title: Conduct AI Threat Modeling and Intelligence
intro: Thinking like an attacker, systematically: choosing and applying threat modelling methods such as STRIDE, PASTA and MAESTRO across AI pipelines; profiling human and non-human threat actors, their objectives and insider threats; understanding the classic adversarial machine learning attacks; mapping threats specific to generative AI, RAG, agents and multimodal systems; and planning for availability attacks that exhaust compute and tokens.
objectives: Select and apply threat modelling methods (STRIDE, PASTA, MAESTRO) across the full AI pipeline, using threat libraries
Profile AI threat actors by motivation, capability and access, including insiders and non-human actors
Explain evasion, poisoning, backdoors, model extraction, model inversion and membership inference, and their defences
Identify threats specific to generative AI, RAG, agentic workflows and multimodal systems, using the OWASP lists
Recognise compute and token exhaustion attacks, and design layered defences against them
Explain how evasion and privacy attacks work in depth, and judge whether a robustness evaluation is credible

sections.title: Threat modelling methodologies for AI pipelines

blocks.title: Choosing how to threat model AI

scenes.title: Choosing how to threat model AI
scenes.sub: STRIDE, PASTA, MAESTRO and the threat libraries behind them
scenes.say: Threat modelling asks four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job? For AI, the second question has many new answers. | This video compares three methodologies, STRIDE, PASTA and MAESTRO, and shows how to apply them across an AI pipeline.

scenes.title: Three methodologies
scenes.say: Three methodologies are especially useful for AI. | STRIDE focuses on categories of threat. PASTA focuses on risk, simulating how attacks would unfold. MAESTRO focuses on the layers of agentic AI systems. | STRIDE is applied to each element and data flow in a diagram. PASTA works through seven stages, starting from business objectives. MAESTRO examines seven layers, and the threats that cross between them. | STRIDE suits everyday design reviews of any system. PASTA suits high-value systems that justify deeper analysis. And MAESTRO suits agents and multi-agent systems.

scenes.title: MAESTRO’s seven layers
scenes.say: MAESTRO, from the Cloud Security Alliance, models agentic systems in seven layers. | Layer one: the foundation models that agents reason with. | Layer two: data operations, including retrieval, embeddings and memory. | Layer three: agent frameworks, the orchestration, tools and protocols. | Layer four: deployment and infrastructure. | Layer five: evaluation and observability. | Layer six: security and compliance, which cuts across all the others. | And layer seven: the agent ecosystem, where agents, users and services interact. MAESTRO asks for threats in each layer, and especially threats that cross layers, such as a poisoned memory in layer two hijacking a tool in layer three.

scenes.title: Threats along an AI pipeline
scenes.say: Whatever method you use, apply it across the whole pipeline, not just the deployed application. Data sourcing faces poisoning, and licensing or consent problems. | Training faces backdoors and tampered training code. | The model registry faces swapped or unsigned models. | Deployment faces compromise of the pipeline that ships models. | Inference faces prompt injection, extraction and abuse. | And monitoring itself faces evasion and log tampering. Each stage has its own trust boundaries, owners and controls.

scenes.title: Threat libraries to draw on
scenes.say: Methodologies tell you how to look. Threat libraries tell you what to look for. | MITRE ATLAS catalogues adversary tactics, techniques and real case studies. | The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications lists the main risks for applications built on language models. | The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications does the same for agents. | NIST AI 100-2 provides a taxonomy of adversarial machine learning attacks and mitigations. | Incident databases record real AI failures and attacks. | And threat intelligence from AI providers and sector groups shows what attackers are doing now.

items: STRIDE for categories, PASTA for risk, MAESTRO for agent layers
Model the whole pipeline, not just the app
Draw threats from ATLAS, OWASP, NIST and intelligence
Look for cross-layer threats in agentic systems
scenes.say: To recap. | Use STRIDE for threat categories, PASTA for risk-driven attack simulation, and MAESTRO for the layers of agentic systems. | Model the whole pipeline, from data sourcing to monitoring, not just the deployed application. | Draw threats from ATLAS, the OWASP lists, NIST AI 100-2 and current threat intelligence. | And in agentic systems, look especially for threats that cross layers.

blocks.md:
### The methodologies in more detail
**STRIDE** (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is applied to each element and data flow in a data flow diagram (Module 4.1). It is fast and widely understood, but it doesn’t rank risk on its own, and AI-specific threats need to be mapped into its categories (for example, prompt injection as tampering with instructions, extraction as information disclosure).

**PASTA** (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) is a risk-centric, seven-stage method:
1. Define business objectives.
2. Define the technical scope.
3. Decompose the application.
4. Analyse threats (using intelligence).
5. Analyse vulnerabilities and weaknesses.
6. Model attacks (attack trees and simulations).
7. Analyse risk and impact, and decide on countermeasures.

It links threats to business impact, which suits high-value AI systems such as fraud models or customer-facing agents, but it takes more effort.

**MAESTRO** (Multi-Agent Environment, Security, Threat, Risk and Outcome), published by the Cloud Security Alliance in 2025, extends earlier methods for **agentic AI**. It decomposes a system into seven layers (foundation models; data operations; agent frameworks; deployment and infrastructure; evaluation and observability; security and compliance; agent ecosystem), identifies threats per layer and **across layers**, and prioritises them by likelihood and impact.

**Other useful methods:** **LINDDUN** for privacy threats, **attack trees** for detailed attack paths, and **kill chain analysis** using ATLAS tactics (Module 5.6).

### Making threat modelling work for AI
- **Scope the whole life cycle:** data sourcing, labelling, training, evaluation, registry, deployment, inference, agents and tools, monitoring and retirement.
- **Include non-human actors:** agents, tools, MCP servers and other organisations’ agents in an ecosystem (Section 2).
- **Use threat libraries:** MITRE ATLAS, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025), the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), NIST AI 100-2 E2025, incident databases and provider threat reports.
- **Revisit on change:** new models, data sources, tools or autonomy, and new threat intelligence, should trigger an update (Module 5.4).
- **Produce usable outputs:** each threat should map to a risk register entry, controls with owners, and tests that prove the controls work (Modules 6.4 and 6.6).
- **Threat modelling as code:** open-source tools such as OWASP Threat Dragon, pytm and Threagile keep models versioned alongside the system.

blocks.title: Methodology questions
blocks.md: Know what each method is for: **STRIDE** (threat categories per element), **PASTA** (seven risk-centric stages linked to business objectives), **MAESTRO** (seven layers for agentic AI, with **cross-layer** threats), **LINDDUN** (privacy). The best answers model the **whole AI life cycle**, use **threat libraries** such as ATLAS and OWASP, and **update the model when things change**.

q.q: A team is threat modelling a multi-agent system in which agents share memory and call tools through MCP. Which approach is MOST suitable?
o: A STRIDE review of the web front end only, since that is where users interact
MAESTRO, examining each layer and the threats that cross between layers
A penetration test of the servers instead of any threat modelling
LINDDUN only, because the main risk in agent systems is always to privacy
q.why: MAESTRO is designed for agentic systems, and cross-layer threats, such as poisoned memory hijacking tool use, are central to multi-agent risk. A front-end-only review, a server test or a privacy-only method miss most of the threats.

sections.title: AI threat actors, objectives and insider threats

blocks.title: Who wants to attack your AI, and why

scenes.title: Who wants to attack your AI, and why
scenes.sub: Threat actors, objectives and insider threats
scenes.say: Good threat models start with the adversary: who might attack, what they want, what they can do, and what access they already have. With AI, some of those adversaries aren’t human at all. | This video covers AI threat actors, their objectives, and insider threats, both human and non-human.

scenes.title: What attackers want from AI systems

items.d: Make the model do their bidding
Extract data or the model itself

scenes.say: Attackers want six broad things from AI systems. | To break availability: degrading or denying the service. | To violate integrity: making the model produce the outputs, or take the actions, they choose. | To compromise privacy: extracting training data, user data or the model itself. | To enable misuse: bypassing safety controls to produce harmful content. NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy uses these first four as its attacker goals. | To make money, through fraud, reselling access or stealing compute. | And to gain strategic advantage, through espionage, intellectual property theft or influence operations.

scenes.title: Actors by access and capability
scenes.say: Two dimensions help profile actors: their access, and their capability. | Inside access with high capability is the most dangerous combination: a malicious insider with machine learning skills, who can poison data, plant backdoors or copy weights. | Inside access with lower capability: careless employees who paste sensitive data into public tools, or staff whose accounts are compromised. | Outside access with high capability: state-linked and organised criminal groups, who research AI systems and automate their attacks. | And outside access with lower capability: opportunistic abusers trying published jailbreaks or stolen keys.

scenes.title: Non-human threat actors
scenes.say: Some threat actors aren’t people. | Compromised agents, hijacked by content they read, act with your own permissions. | Rogue agents act outside their purpose, through misconfiguration or misaligned behaviour. | Malicious tools and servers, such as a poisoned MCP server or plugin, sit inside your agents’ trust boundary. | External agents, belonging to partners or customers, interact with yours in multi-agent ecosystems. | Bots and automation scrape content and stuff credentials at scale. | And AI-powered attack tools automate reconnaissance, phishing and exploitation. In November 2025, Anthropic reported disrupting an espionage campaign, attributed to a Chinese state-sponsored group, in which its AI coding tool carried out most of the operational work.

scenes.title: Insider threats to AI

items.d: Theft of models or data; sabotage
Sensitive data in public AI tools

scenes.say: Insider threats to AI take five forms, and need a sixth thing: controls. | Malicious insiders steal models or data, or sabotage pipelines. In 2024, US prosecutors charged a former Google engineer with stealing trade secrets about the company’s AI infrastructure. | Negligent insiders put sensitive data into public AI tools. | Compromised insiders have their credentials stolen and used by others. | Departing staff may take weights, prompts or datasets with them. | Third-party insiders, such as contractors and data labellers, have privileged access too. | Controls include least privilege, monitoring of access to weights and data, separation of duties and thorough offboarding.

items: Attacker goals: availability, integrity, privacy, misuse, money, advantage
Profile actors by access and capability
Include non-human actors: agents, tools, bots, AI attack tools
Insiders: malicious, negligent, compromised, departing, third-party
scenes.say: To recap. | Attackers target availability, integrity, privacy and safety controls, for money or strategic advantage. | Profile actors by their access and their capability. | Include non-human actors: compromised and rogue agents, malicious tools, bots and AI-powered attack tools. | And plan for every kind of insider: malicious, negligent, compromised, departing and third-party.

blocks.md:
### Threat actor profiles
| Actor | Typical motivation | Capabilities | Likely AI targets |
|---|---|---|---|
| **State-linked groups** | Espionage, strategic advantage, influence | High: research, custom tooling, patience, AI-assisted operations | Model weights and research, sensitive data via AI systems, influence campaigns using generative AI |
| **Organised criminals** | Money | Moderate to high: fraud, ransomware, resale of access | Stolen API keys and compute, fraud with deepfakes, extortion using stolen data |
| **Competitors and IP thieves** | Advantage | Moderate: systematic querying, recruitment of insiders | Model extraction and distillation, training data |
| **Hacktivists** | Ideology, publicity | Low to moderate | Jailbreaks for embarrassing outputs, disruption |
| **Malicious insiders** | Money, grievance, coercion | Legitimate access and knowledge | Weights, datasets, pipelines, backdoors |
| **Opportunistic abusers** | Curiosity, free use, mischief | Low; rely on published techniques | Public chatbots, exposed endpoints and keys |
| **Non-human actors** | (Inherited from whoever controls them) | Machine speed, legitimate permissions | Tools, data and systems the agent can reach |

### Objectives in NIST AI 100-2
NIST’s taxonomy of adversarial machine learning (AI 100-2 E2025) classifies attacks by the attacker’s **goals** (availability breakdown, integrity violation, privacy compromise, and, for generative AI, misuse enablement), their **capabilities** (such as control of training data, the model, queries or resources the model reads) and their **knowledge** (white-box, grey-box or black-box). Using these dimensions in threat models makes assumptions explicit.

### Insider threat controls for AI
- **Least privilege and just-in-time access** to weights, training data and pipelines (Module 4.6).
- **Separation of duties** for training, approval and deployment, so one person can’t plant and ship a backdoor (Module 5.1).
- **Monitoring** of access to weights and datasets, bulk downloads, use of personal storage and unusual AI tool use (Module 5.3).
- **Data loss prevention** and approved AI tools, so staff have a safe alternative to public services (Module 2.6).
- **Joiner, mover and leaver processes** that remove access promptly and recover assets (Module 4.7).
- **Third parties:** contractual controls, vetting and monitoring for labellers, contractors and vendors (Module 6.3).
- **Culture and reporting:** training, clear policies and safe ways to raise concerns. CISA’s insider threat guidance emphasises a multidisciplinary programme involving HR, legal and security.

### Non-human actors
Treat agents, tools and external agents as **potential adversaries** in threat models: what could each do with its permissions if it were compromised or misbehaving? This is the basis for least agency, approvals for high-impact actions and agent monitoring (Modules 4.6 and 5.3).

blocks.title: Actor and objective terms
cards: Integrity violation
An attack that makes a model produce outputs or take actions the attacker chooses.
Misuse enablement
Bypassing a generative model’s safety controls to obtain harmful output.
White-box attacker
An attacker who knows the model’s architecture and weights.
Negligent insider
A staff member who causes harm without intent, such as pasting secrets into a public AI tool.
Non-human threat actor
An agent, tool, server or bot that acts against your interests, whoever controls it.

blocks.title: Threat actor questions
blocks.md: Profile actors by **motivation, capability and access**, and include **non-human actors** (compromised agents, malicious tools, external agents). For insiders, the strongest controls combine **least privilege, separation of duties, monitoring of weights and data, and offboarding**. Know NIST AI 100-2’s attacker goals: **availability, integrity, privacy and misuse**.

q.q: A data scientist with access to training pipelines resigns to join a competitor. Which control would MOST reduce the risk of model or data theft during their notice period?
o: Ask them to sign a statement confirming that they won’t take any company data
Reduce access to what is still needed, and monitor weight and dataset downloads
Allow full access to continue, so their handover work isn’t interrupted
Wait until their last day and then disable all of their accounts at once
q.why: Narrowing access and monitoring sensitive downloads limits what can be taken and detects attempts. Statements don’t prevent theft, full access keeps the risk, and waiting until the last day leaves the notice period exposed.

scenes.title: Attacks on the model itself
scenes.sub: Evasion, poisoning, extraction, inversion and backdoors
scenes.say: Long before chatbots, researchers showed that machine learning models could be fooled, corrupted and copied. These adversarial machine learning attacks apply to every kind of model, from fraud scoring to vision to language. | This video covers the five classic families: evasion, poisoning, backdoors, model extraction, and model inversion with membership inference.

scenes.title: Five families of adversarial ML attack

layers.label: Evasion
layers.sub: Crafted inputs cause wrong outputs at inference

layers.label: Poisoning
layers.sub: Corrupted training data degrades or steers the model

layers.label: Backdoors
layers.sub: A hidden trigger activates attacker-chosen behaviour

layers.label: Model extraction
layers.sub: Queries used to copy the model’s functionality

layers.label: Inversion and membership inference
layers.sub: Outputs reveal training data or who was in it

scenes.say: There are five families. | Evasion: carefully crafted inputs make a deployed model give wrong answers, such as small changes that make malware look benign to a classifier. | Poisoning: corrupted training data degrades the model generally, or steers it in targeted ways. | Backdoors: a hidden trigger, planted through training data or the model itself, activates behaviour the attacker chose, while the model behaves normally otherwise. | Model extraction: an attacker uses many queries to build a copy of the model’s functionality. | And inversion and membership inference: outputs reveal information about the training data, or whether a particular person’s data was used.

scenes.title: What the attacker knows
scenes.say: The attacker’s knowledge shapes the attack. | A white-box attacker knows the architecture and weights. A grey-box attacker knows some details, such as the model family. A black-box attacker sees only inputs and outputs. | White-box attackers can compute precise evasion inputs from the model’s gradients. Grey-box attackers often build a proxy model and transfer attacks from it. Black-box attackers rely on queries, for example to extract the model. | So defences differ: protect the weights from white-box access, limit what you disclose about models, and limit query volumes and output detail against black-box attacks.

scenes.title: Why output detail and query limits matter
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative agreement between a stolen copy and the original model
scenes.say: This illustrative chart shows how extraction depends on what the attacker can see. When an API returns full probability scores, a stolen copy agrees with the original more and more closely as queries increase. | Returning only the top label gives the attacker far less to learn from, so the copy improves more slowly. | And rate limits cap the number of queries in the first place. Output minimisation and query limits work together against extraction and inversion.

scenes.title: How a backdoor works
scenes.say: Here is how a backdoor works. The attacker plants trigger samples: training examples that pair a rare pattern with the outcome they want, or direct changes to a model’s weights. | The model learns the association between the trigger and the target behaviour. | Because the trigger is rare, the model passes normal evaluation, with clean accuracy unchanged. | It is deployed, and behaves normally for everyone else. | Then the trigger appears in an input, perhaps a particular phrase, image patch or code pattern. | And the model produces the attacker’s chosen behaviour: a misclassification, a data leak, or, for an agent, an action.

items: Evasion, poisoning, backdoors, extraction, inversion and membership inference
Attacker knowledge: white-box, grey-box, black-box
Limit outputs and queries against extraction and inversion
Backdoors pass normal tests: protect data and model provenance
scenes.say: To recap. | The five classic families are evasion, poisoning, backdoors, model extraction, and inversion with membership inference. | What the attacker knows, white-box, grey-box or black-box, shapes both attack and defence. | Limit output detail and query volumes against extraction and inversion. | And because backdoors pass normal testing, protect the provenance of data and models, and test for triggers.

blocks.md:
### Adversarial ML attack families
| Attack | Stage | Goal | Landmark research | Key defences (Module 6.6) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Evasion** | Inference | Integrity | Physical adversarial examples made road-sign classifiers misread stop signs (Eykholt et al., 2018) | Adversarial training, input preprocessing, ensembles, robustness testing |
| **Poisoning** | Training | Availability or integrity | Indiscriminate and targeted poisoning studies; web-scale poisoning shown practical (Carlini et al., 2023) | Data provenance and validation, robust training, anomaly detection (Module 3.3) |
| **Backdoors** | Training or supply chain | Integrity | BadNets showed hidden triggers surviving normal evaluation (Gu et al., 2017) | Provenance, signed models, trigger scanning, fine-pruning, red teaming |
| **Model extraction** | Inference | Privacy (of the model) | Stealing models through prediction APIs (Tramèr et al., 2016); extracting part of a production language model (Carlini et al., 2024) | Rate limits, output minimisation, query monitoring, watermarking and fingerprinting (Module 3.6) |
| **Model inversion** | Inference | Privacy (of training data) | Reconstructing recognisable faces from a face recognition model (Fredrikson et al., 2015) | Output minimisation, differential privacy, access control |
| **Membership inference** | Inference | Privacy | Inferring whether a record was in the training set (Shokri et al., 2017) | Differential privacy, regularisation, output minimisation |
| **Training data extraction** | Inference | Privacy | Extracting memorised training text from GPT-2 (Carlini et al., 2021) | Deduplication, differential privacy, output filtering (Module 3.3) |

### Attacker capabilities and knowledge
NIST AI 100-2 E2025 describes attacker **capabilities**: control of training data, labels, the model or its source code, query access to the deployed model, and (for generative AI) control of resources the model reads, such as web pages and documents. Combined with **knowledge** (white-box, grey-box, black-box), these define realistic scenarios for threat models and red teams.

### Applying this to modern systems
- **Language models** face all these families: evasion appears as jailbreaks and adversarial suffixes; poisoning and backdoors through pre-training, fine-tuning and retrieval data; extraction through distillation; and training data extraction through memorisation.
- **Fine-tuned and open-weight models** expose white-box access to anyone who downloads them, so supply chain provenance matters (Module 6.3).
- **Predictive models** in fraud, security and vision remain prime evasion targets, because attackers directly benefit from misclassification.

pairs: Stickers on a road sign make a vision model misread it
Evasion
A rare phrase in the input makes a code model insert a flaw
Backdoor
Thousands of API queries are used to train a copycat model
Model extraction
An attacker tests whether a patient’s record was in the training data
Membership inference
Mislabelled samples are slipped into a fraud model’s training set
Poisoning

blocks.title: Adversarial ML questions
blocks.md: Match each attack to its **stage** (training or inference) and **goal** (availability, integrity, privacy). **Evasion** happens at inference; **poisoning and backdoors** at training; **extraction, inversion and membership inference** abuse query access. Defences follow: **provenance** for training-time attacks, **output minimisation and rate limits** for query attacks, **adversarial training and robustness testing** for evasion.

q.q: A company’s fraud model API returns full probability scores to any authenticated partner, without rate limits. Which attack does this MOST directly enable?
o: A backdoor planted in the model’s training data by a malicious insider
Model extraction, by training a copy on large numbers of query results
Data poisoning of the training pipeline through the partner interface
A denial of service attack against the company’s web front end
q.why: Unlimited queries with detailed outputs give an attacker ideal material to train a copy of the model. Backdoors and poisoning need training-time access, and the scenario doesn’t describe the web front end.

sections.title: Threats specific to generative AI and RAG

blocks.title: New attack surfaces in language and retrieval

scenes.title: New attack surfaces in language and retrieval
scenes.sub: Threats specific to generative AI and RAG
scenes.say: Generative AI changes the attack surface. Instructions and data travel in the same channel, outputs are generated rather than templated, and retrieval pulls in content nobody reviewed. | This video covers threats specific to generative AI and retrieval-augmented generation.

scenes.title: Why generative AI is different
rows: Generated; may hold code or links
scenes.say: Generative AI applications differ from traditional ones in four ways. | Traditional inputs are structured fields that can be validated. Generative AI takes free text, files and images. | Traditional logic is deterministic code. Here, a model follows whatever text it is given, including text an attacker wrote. | Traditional outputs are templated. Generated outputs can contain code, links or markup that downstream systems might execute. | And instead of specific database queries, retrieval pulls whole documents into the model’s context.

scenes.title: Core generative AI threats
scenes.say: Six threats stand out for generative AI. | Prompt injection, direct from users or indirect through content the model reads. | Sensitive data disclosure: training data, retrieved context or system prompts appearing in outputs. | Improper output handling, where generated code, links or markup are executed by downstream systems. | Package hallucination: models invent software packages that don’t exist, and attackers register those names with malicious code. | Misinformation: confident errors that people or systems rely on. | And unbounded consumption: abuse of cost and capacity, covered later in this module.

scenes.title: A hallucinated package

msgs.t: Which Python package should I use to parse CSV files safely?
Use securecsv-parse. Install it with pip, then call its safe_read function.
Package registry: securecsv-parse was registered last week by an unknown account.

notes.d: A developer asks for a library recommendation.
The model recommends a package that never existed. Models often repeat the same invented names.
Attackers watch for repeated hallucinated names and publish malicious packages under them. Verify packages before installing.

scenes.say: Here is package hallucination in action. A developer asks a coding assistant which package to use for parsing CSV files safely. | The assistant confidently recommends a package that never existed. Models often repeat the same invented names, so they are predictable. | Attackers watch for those names and register them, with malicious code inside. The defence is simple but essential: verify that recommended packages exist, are established and come from an approved registry, before anyone installs them.

scenes.title: Attacks specific to RAG
scenes.say: RAG systems add six specific attacks. Knowledge poisoning: research presented in 2025, called PoisonedRAG, showed that five crafted documents per target question, hidden among millions, could steer answers about ninety per cent of the time. | Retrieval manipulation: documents written to rank first for common queries. | Injection carriers: retrieved documents that contain instructions for the model. | Permission bypass: retrieval that ignores document access controls, exposing content users shouldn’t see. | Embedding inversion: vectors that leak much of the text they were made from. | And citation spoofing: planted sources that lend false authority to an answer.

items: GenAI mixes instructions and data, and generates its outputs
Injection, disclosure, output handling, package hallucination, misinformation
RAG: poisoning, rank manipulation, carriers, permission bypass, inversion
A few crafted documents can steer a large knowledge base
scenes.say: To recap. | Generative AI mixes instructions and data in one channel, and generates outputs that may be executed downstream. | Key threats include prompt injection, sensitive data disclosure, improper output handling, package hallucination and misinformation. | RAG adds knowledge poisoning, retrieval manipulation, injection carriers, permission bypass, embedding inversion and citation spoofing. | And remember that a handful of crafted documents can steer answers from a very large knowledge base.

blocks.md:
### The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)
| ID | Risk | In brief |
|---|---|---|
| LLM01 | Prompt Injection | Inputs, direct or indirect, alter the model’s behaviour or output |
| LLM02 | Sensitive Information Disclosure | Personal data, secrets or confidential data exposed through outputs |
| LLM03 | Supply Chain | Compromised models, datasets, packages and platforms (Module 6.3) |
| LLM04 | Data and Model Poisoning | Manipulated pre-training, fine-tuning or embedding data |
| LLM05 | Improper Output Handling | Outputs passed to other systems without validation |
| LLM06 | Excessive Agency | Too much functionality, permission or autonomy (Section 5) |
| LLM07 | System Prompt Leakage | Instructions or secrets in system prompts exposed |
| LLM08 | Vector and Embedding Weaknesses | Weaknesses in how embeddings are generated, stored or retrieved |
| LLM09 | Misinformation | False or misleading outputs relied upon |
| LLM10 | Unbounded Consumption | Excessive use causing denial of service or cost (Section 6) |

### RAG-specific threats
- **Knowledge poisoning:** PoisonedRAG (USENIX Security 2025) injected five malicious texts per target question into knowledge bases of millions of texts and achieved around 90% attack success; the existing defences it tested were insufficient.
- **Retrieval manipulation:** content optimised to be retrieved, including hidden text and keyword stuffing.
- **Indirect injection:** retrieved documents carrying instructions (Module 5.3).
- **Permission bypass and cross-tenant leakage:** retrieval must enforce the user’s permissions **before** content reaches the model (Module 4.1).
- **Embedding inversion:** embeddings can reveal much of their source text, so they deserve the same protection (Module 5.2).
- **Stale or tampered indexes:** outdated content and unlogged changes (Module 5.3).

### Package hallucination
Code assistants sometimes recommend packages that don’t exist. Research has found that hallucinated names recur across prompts, so attackers can predict and register them ("slopsquatting"). In 2024, a researcher who uploaded an empty package under a name models kept hallucinating saw it downloaded thousands of times. Controls: verify packages exist and are established, use internal mirrors with allow-lists, and scan dependencies (Module 6.3).

blocks.title: Which OWASP LLM risk is this?
pairs: Generated SQL is run against the database without validation
LLM05 Improper Output Handling
A user extracts the assistant’s instructions, which contain an API key
LLM07 System Prompt Leakage
Retrieval returns documents from another customer’s tenant
LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses

LLM09 Misinformation

blocks.title: GenAI threat questions
blocks.md: Know the **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)** by name and example. For RAG, remember that **a few poisoned documents can be enough**, that permissions must be enforced **before retrieval results reach the model**, and that **embeddings are sensitive**. Package hallucination is a supply chain risk: **verify before installing**.

q.q: A RAG assistant indexes every document in a shared drive, then filters out restricted documents from its answers after the model has generated them. What is the MAIN weakness?
o: Indexing every document makes retrieval slower than it needs to be
Restricted content has already reached the model, so it can leak in outputs
Shared drives can’t legally be used as sources for retrieval systems
Filtering answers afterwards uses too many tokens for each request
q.why: Permissions must be enforced before retrieval results reach the model. Once restricted content is in the context, output filtering is unreliable, and the model may paraphrase or summarise it. Speed, legality and token cost aren’t the main issue.

sections.title: Threats specific to agentic and multimodal systems

blocks.title: Agents that act, models that see and hear

scenes.title: Agents that act, models that see and hear
scenes.sub: Threats specific to agentic and multimodal systems
scenes.say: Agents turn model outputs into actions, and multimodal models take in images, audio and video. Both widen the ways an attacker can reach a model, and the damage it can do. | This video covers threats specific to agentic workflows and multimodal systems.

scenes.title: Leading agentic threats
scenes.say: The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, published in December 2025, names the leading risks. Six of them stand out. | Agent goal hijack: injected content redirects what the agent is trying to achieve. | Tool misuse: legitimate tools used in harmful ways, such as sending data out by email. | Identity and privilege abuse: an agent’s access or delegated credentials exploited. | Memory and context poisoning: planted instructions that persist and affect later sessions. | Insecure communication between agents: spoofed, replayed or tampered messages. | And cascading failures, where one agent’s error spreads through a chain of others.

scenes.title: A cascading failure across agents
scenes.say: Here is how a cascading failure unfolds. A research agent’s memory is poisoned with a false claim about a supplier. | It passes false findings to a planner agent. | The planner builds a plan on those findings, trusting its colleague. | A finance agent executes the payments the plan calls for. | Each step looks normal on its own, so no single alert fires. | And the human approver trusts the agents’ consensus, which the OWASP list calls human-agent trust exploitation. Defences include verifying claims between agents, limiting each agent’s authority, and monitoring whole chains, not just single steps.

scenes.title: Multimodal attack routes
rows: Scan image text; treat it as untrusted
Instructions in metadata or white text
scenes.say: Multimodal models open new routes for attack. | Images can carry hidden text or subtle pixel changes. Treat any text found in images as untrusted input. | Audio can carry disguised or even inaudible commands. Require confirmation for high-impact voice actions. | Video enables deepfakes of real people. Verify requests through a separate channel, and check content provenance. | And documents can hide instructions in metadata or white-on-white text. Strip metadata, and scan what the model will actually read.

scenes.title: A deepfake-enabled payment fraud
scenes.say: Deepfakes have already enabled large frauds. Here is the pattern of a widely reported case. | An employee receives a message, apparently from the chief financial officer, about a confidential transaction. | Suspicious at first, the employee joins a video call, where the CFO and several colleagues all appear and speak. All of them are deepfakes. | Reassured, the employee makes a series of urgent transfers to new accounts. | The fraud is discovered days later, when the employee checks with head office. | The lesson is that process controls beat detection: verify payment requests through a separate, known channel, and require dual approval.

items: Agentic: goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory poisoning
Also: insecure agent messages, cascading failures, trust exploitation
Multimodal: treat text in images, audio and files as untrusted
Deepfakes: rely on out-of-band verification and dual approval
scenes.say: To recap. | Agentic threats include goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and memory poisoning. | They also include insecure communication between agents, cascading failures and exploitation of human trust. | For multimodal systems, treat text found in images, audio and documents as untrusted input. | And against deepfakes, rely on out-of-band verification and dual approval, not on spotting the fake.

blocks.md:
### The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)
Published by the OWASP GenAI Security Project in December 2025:
| ID | Risk | In brief |
|---|---|---|
| ASI01 | Agent Goal Hijack | Injected content or manipulation redirects an agent’s goals |
| ASI02 | Tool Misuse and Exploitation | Legitimate tools used unsafely or for harm |
| ASI03 | Identity and Privilege Abuse | Agent identities, credentials or delegated rights exploited (Module 4.6) |
| ASI04 | Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities | Compromised tools, MCP servers, plugins, models or agent components (Module 6.3) |
| ASI05 | Unexpected Code Execution | Agents generating or running code that leads to compromise |
| ASI06 | Memory and Context Poisoning | Persistent memory or shared context corrupted |
| ASI07 | Insecure Inter-Agent Communication | Spoofed, replayed or tampered messages between agents (for example over A2A) |
| ASI08 | Cascading Failures | Errors or compromise propagating across agents and systems |
| ASI09 | Human-Agent Trust Exploitation | People over-trusting agents, or agents manipulating people |
| ASI10 | Rogue Agents | Agents acting outside their intended purpose or control |

### Protocol-level threats
- **MCP:** tool poisoning (malicious instructions in tool descriptions), tool shadowing (one server interfering with another’s tools), "rug pulls" (a trusted server changing behaviour after approval) and over-privileged servers (Module 4.1).
- **Agent-to-agent (A2A):** agent impersonation, forged agent cards, message tampering and replay, and delegation chains that exceed intended authority. Authenticate agents, sign messages and limit what remote agents may request.

### Multimodal threats
- **Images:** typographic attacks (text in an image that the model reads as an instruction), adversarial perturbations, and instructions hidden in low-contrast text.
- **Audio:** commands hidden in audio, including ultrasonic commands shown to work against voice assistants (DolphinAttack, 2017), and cloned voices.
- **Video and deepfakes:** in early 2024, an employee of engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong transferred about HK$200 million (around US$25 million) after a video call in which the CFO and colleagues were deepfakes.
- **Documents:** hidden text, metadata, comments and embedded objects.
- **Defences:** treat content from every modality as untrusted data; extract and scan text from images and files; require confirmation for high-impact actions; use content provenance standards such as C2PA where available; and design payment and access processes so that a convincing face or voice is never enough (Module 6.6).

blocks.title: Which agentic risk is this?
pairs: An agent’s notes from yesterday contain a planted instruction it follows today
Memory and context poisoning (ASI06)
An email convinces an agent its real task is to export customer data
Agent goal hijack (ASI01)
A remote agent forges another agent’s identity in A2A messages
Insecure inter-agent communication (ASI07)
A trusted MCP server silently changes its tool behaviour after approval
Agentic supply chain vulnerability (ASI04)
An approver signs off because three agents all agreed
Human-agent trust exploitation (ASI09)

blocks.title: Agentic and multimodal questions
blocks.md: Know the **OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)**: goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation and rogue agents. For multimodal systems, **all modalities are untrusted input**. Against deepfakes, the best answer is a **process control** (out-of-band verification, dual approval), not detection alone.

q.q: A finance team uses video calls to approve urgent payments requested by executives. Which control BEST reduces the risk of deepfake fraud?
o: Train staff to look for visual glitches that reveal deepfaked faces
Verify requests through a separate known channel, with dual approval
Only accept video calls from executives who have cameras switched on
Use a deepfake detection tool and approve whatever it marks as genuine
q.why: Out-of-band verification and dual approval work however convincing the fake is. Spotting glitches and detection tools are unreliable as deepfakes improve, and cameras being on proves nothing.

sections.title: Availability attacks: compute and token exhaustion

blocks.title: Running the AI out of resources

scenes.title: Running the AI out of resources
scenes.sub: Availability attacks: compute and token exhaustion
scenes.say: Every AI request consumes expensive compute, and pay-per-token pricing turns abuse into a direct financial loss. Attackers don’t need a huge flood of traffic when a few well-chosen requests can be enormously costly. | This video covers availability attacks on AI systems: compute and token exhaustion.

scenes.title: Ways to exhaust an AI system

items.d: Prompts that force very long answers

scenes.say: There are six main ways to exhaust an AI system. | Token floods: simply sending large volumes of requests. | Context stuffing: filling every request to the maximum input length. | Output amplification: prompts designed to force extremely long answers. | Agent loops: tricking agents into recursive plans or endless cycles of tool calls. | Sponge inputs: inputs crafted to maximise the computation and energy a model uses, shown in research from 2021. | And denial of wallet: driving usage costs past budgets until the service is switched off or the bill becomes the damage.

scenes.title: Some requests cost far more than others
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative thousands of tokens consumed per request
scenes.say: This illustrative chart shows why AI availability attacks don’t need floods. A normal request might use a few thousand tokens. A stuffed context uses a hundred and twenty thousand, output amplification tens of thousands, and a single runaway agent loop hundreds of thousands. One attacker can impose the cost of thousands of normal users.

scenes.title: Traditional DoS and AI exhaustion
scenes.say: AI exhaustion differs from traditional denial of service. | Traditional attacks consume bandwidth and connections. AI attacks consume tokens and GPU seconds. | Traditional attacks need huge floods. AI attacks can work with a few costly requests. | Traditional attacks show up as traffic spikes. AI attacks show up as cost and token anomalies, often from authenticated users. | And where traditional defences use scrubbing services and content delivery networks, AI defences rely on quotas, caps and budgets.

scenes.title: Layered defences against exhaustion
scenes.say: Defences come in layers. Start with identity and quotas per user, key and tenant, so no anonymous caller can consume unlimited resources. | Limit inputs: size, number of files and request rate. | Cap outputs with maximum token limits. | Give agents budgets for steps, time and cost per task. | Use anomaly-based circuit breakers on cost and token usage. | And isolate capacity, with separate queues for critical services and tenants, so one abuser can’t starve everyone else.

items: Floods, stuffing, amplification, loops, sponges, denial of wallet
A few costly requests can do the damage
Watch cost and token anomalies, not just traffic
Quotas, input and output caps, agent budgets, breakers, isolation
scenes.say: To recap. | AI availability attacks include token floods, context stuffing, output amplification, agent loops, sponge inputs and denial of wallet. | A few costly requests can do as much damage as a large flood. | Detect them through cost and token anomalies, not just traffic volume. | And defend in layers: quotas, input and output caps, agent budgets, circuit breakers and capacity isolation.

blocks.md:
### Availability threats in the frameworks
- **OWASP LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption** covers excessive and uncontrolled inference: denial of service, denial of wallet, model extraction through unlimited queries, and resource-intensive inputs.
- **MITRE ATLAS** includes techniques such as denial of AI service and cost harvesting.
- **NIST AI 100-2** classifies availability breakdown as one of the attacker’s goals, including energy-latency attacks such as **sponge examples** (Shumailov et al., 2021), inputs crafted to maximise a model’s energy use and latency.

### Attack patterns and defences
| Pattern | Example | Defences |
|---|---|---|
| **Token floods** | Automated scripts with stolen or free-tier keys | Authentication, per-identity quotas, rate limits, bot detection |
| **Context stuffing** | Every request at the maximum context length | Input size limits, document size and count limits, pricing tiers |
| **Output amplification** | Prompts demanding exhaustive, repetitive answers | Maximum output tokens, response length policies |
| **Agent loops** | Injected instructions that make an agent call tools endlessly | Step, time and cost budgets per task; loop detection (Module 4.7) |
| **Retrieval exhaustion** | Expensive vector searches or huge result sets | Query limits, top-k caps, caching |
| **GPU and queue exhaustion** | Saturating shared inference capacity | Capacity isolation, priority queues, autoscaling with limits |
| **Denial of wallet** | Running up provider bills | Budgets and hard caps, spend alerts, circuit breakers (Module 5.7) |

### Planning for availability
- **Include availability in threat models** from the start, with explicit assumptions about who can call the system and how often.
- **Separate critical workloads** from experimental or public ones, so abuse of one can’t starve the other.
- **Watch the business signal:** cost per hour, tokens per identity and queue depth are often the earliest indicators (Module 5.2).
- **Test it:** include resource exhaustion scenarios in red teaming and load testing (Module 6.4).
- **Plan for provider limits:** your provider’s rate limits are shared across your applications; one abusive feature can exhaust the quota for all of them (Module 5.7).

blocks.title: Availability terms
cards: Denial of wallet
An attack that drives usage costs up until budgets are exhausted or the service is switched off.
Context stuffing
Filling requests to the maximum input length to increase cost and latency.
Sponge example
An input crafted to maximise a model’s computation, energy use and latency.
Agent budget
Limits on the steps, time and cost an agent may spend on a single task.
Capacity isolation
Separate queues or capacity for critical services, so abuse of one can’t starve others.

blocks.title: Availability questions
blocks.md: For AI, think **cost as well as capacity**. The best answers apply **per-identity quotas**, **input and output token caps**, **agent step and cost budgets**, **cost anomaly detection with circuit breakers**, and **capacity isolation**. Traditional DDoS protection alone doesn’t stop a few authenticated, very expensive requests.

q.q: A public AI assistant suffers huge provider bills from a small number of accounts sending maximum-length documents and asking for exhaustive answers. Which combination of controls is MOST effective?
o: A content delivery network in front of the assistant to absorb traffic
Per-account quotas, input size limits, output token caps and spend alerts
A larger monthly budget with the provider, so the service stays online
A CAPTCHA on the home page, shown once per browser session
q.why: The problem is cost per request from known accounts, so per-account quotas, input and output limits and spend alerts address it directly. A CDN and CAPTCHA don’t limit costly authenticated requests, and a bigger budget just pays for the abuse.

sections.title: Deep dive: adversarial examples and privacy attacks

scenes.title: How adversarial attacks really work
scenes.sub: Perturbation budgets, gradient attacks and privacy attacks
scenes.say: Section three named the families of adversarial machine learning attacks. This deep dive shows how the main ones actually work: how attackers define a small change, how they use gradients to find one, and how privacy attacks decide whether a person’s data was used. | Knowing the mechanics is what lets you judge whether a robustness claim, or a test report, can be trusted.

scenes.title: How small is “small”? Perturbation budgets
scenes.say: Attacks are defined against a perturbation budget, epsilon, measured with a norm. The three common norms limit different things. | The L-infinity norm limits the largest change to any single value. The L-two norm limits the overall size of the change. The L-zero norm limits how many values change at all. | Typical budgets: for images, often eight two-hundred-and-fifty-fifths per pixel under L-infinity; a small total distance under L-two; or just a handful of pixels under L-zero. | Each norm has its classic attacks: FGSM and PGD for L-infinity, Carlini and Wagner’s attack for L-two, and sparse attacks for L-zero. Physical attacks, such as stickers on a sign, are better described as patches: large changes confined to a small area.

scenes.title: FGSM and PGD: following the gradient
scenes.say: A white-box evasion attack starts with an input the model gets right, such as a photo of a stop sign. | The attacker computes the gradient of the model’s loss with respect to the input, not the weights. It shows which tiny change to each pixel would increase the error most. | The fast gradient sign method, FGSM, takes a single step: it moves every pixel by epsilon in the direction of the gradient’s sign. It is quick, but often weak. | Projected gradient descent, PGD, takes many smaller steps from a random starting point, and projects back inside the budget after each one. It is the standard strong attack for testing defences. | The result looks unchanged to a person, but the model misclassifies it. Optimisation attacks, such as Carlini and Wagner’s, search for the smallest change that works.

scenes.title: Accuracy falls as the budget grows
scenes.yLabel: Accuracy under a strong attack, by L∞ budget (illustrative)
scenes.say: Robustness is reported as a curve, not a single number. An undefended image classifier may score ninety-four per cent on clean images, yet fall close to zero once a strong attack has even a small budget. | A model trained with adversarial examples starts lower on clean images, but holds up far better as the budget grows, though it still fails eventually. | Many benchmarks report accuracy at one budget, often eight two-hundred-and-fifty-fifths. Be wary of results that look too good: if accuracy never reaches zero as the budget grows, or one-step attacks beat many-step ones, the defence may simply be hiding its gradients.

scenes.title: Membership inference with shadow models
scenes.say: Membership inference asks whether a particular record was used to train a model. The classic attack starts with data similar to the target’s training data. | The attacker trains shadow models on parts of it, so for every shadow model they know exactly which records were members. | By comparing the shadow models’ outputs on members and non-members, they learn the tell-tale signs, such as unusually high confidence on training examples. | Then they query the target model with the record in question, and pass its output to the attack. | The verdict is member or not. Strong modern attacks, such as the likelihood ratio attack, LiRA, are judged by how many members they find while keeping false positives very rare, because a confident hit on one person is the real privacy harm.

items: Norm budgets define how small “small” is
FGSM takes one gradient step; PGD takes many
Test with strong, adaptive attacks, never weak ones
Judge membership inference at low false-positive rates
scenes.say: To recap. | Perturbation budgets, measured with norms such as L-infinity and L-two, define how small a change has to be. | FGSM takes one step along the input gradient; PGD takes many projected steps, and is the stronger test. | Robustness claims need strong, adaptive attacks and a full accuracy curve, never a single weak attack. | And membership inference is judged by the members it finds at a very low false-positive rate.

blocks.md:
### Threat models for evasion
An evasion attack searches for an input close to a real one that the model gets wrong. “Close” is set by a **perturbation budget** (ε) under a norm: **L∞** limits the largest change to any single value (for images, often 8/255 per pixel), **L2** limits the overall size of the change, and **L0** limits how many values change. Physical attacks, such as stickers on a road sign, are better described as **patches**: large changes confined to a small area, designed to survive printing, distance and viewing angle. **Targeted** attacks aim for a chosen output; **untargeted** attacks for any wrong one.

### White-box attacks
- **FGSM** (Goodfellow et al., 2015): one step of size ε in the direction of the sign of the input gradient. Fast but weak; mainly used for quick checks and cheap adversarial training.
- **PGD** (Madry et al., 2018): many small steps from a random start, each projected back into the budget. The standard strong first-order attack, and the basis of adversarial training (Module 6.6).
- **Carlini–Wagner** (2017): an optimisation that searches for a minimal perturbation. It defeated defensive distillation, a defence published the year before.
- **AutoAttack** (Croce and Hein, 2020): an ensemble of parameter-free attacks, used as a reliable benchmark by leaderboards such as RobustBench.

### Black-box routes
| Route | What the attacker needs | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Transfer** | A similar substitute model | Craft examples on the substitute; many also fool the target |
| **Score-based** | Confidence scores | Estimate gradients from how the scores change |
| **Decision-based** | Labels only | Walk along the decision boundary, as HopSkipJump does |

Returning labels instead of scores, rate limiting and query monitoring raise the cost of score-based and decision-based attacks (Module 3.6). Transfer attacks need no queries to the target at all, which is why openly available models make useful substitutes. **Universal perturbations** fool a model on most inputs at once, and the same optimisation ideas underpin adversarial suffixes against language models (Module 6.4).

### Evaluating robustness honestly
Athalye, Carlini and Wagner (2018) found that 7 of 9 defences accepted at ICLR 2018 relied on **obfuscated gradients**, which defeat weak attacks but not adaptive ones; they circumvented 6 completely and 1 partially. Warning signs include one-step attacks beating iterative ones, black-box attacks beating white-box ones, and accuracy that never reaches zero as the budget grows. Ask for **adaptive attacks** designed against the specific defence, strong iterative attacks such as PGD and AutoAttack, and the full curve of accuracy against budget.

### Privacy attacks in more depth
- **Membership inference:** Shokri et al. (2017) trained **shadow models** to learn what members look like. The **likelihood ratio attack (LiRA)** (Carlini et al., 2022) compares a record’s loss under many models trained with and without it, and is about ten times more powerful at low false-positive rates. Report the **true-positive rate at a low false-positive rate**, such as 0.1%, rather than average accuracy.
- **Training data extraction:** generate many outputs, then rank them by signs of memorisation. Nasr et al. (2023) showed that an aligned production chatbot could be pushed to diverge from its normal behaviour and emit memorised training data about 150 times more often.
- **Model inversion and attribute inference:** use outputs to reconstruct representative inputs, or to infer sensitive attributes of a known person.
- **Model stealing:** Carlini et al. (2024) recovered the final projection layer of two production language models through their public API for under $20, using log-probabilities and logit bias. OpenAI and Google then changed their APIs to mitigate the attack.

blocks.title: Name the technique
pairs: One step of size ε along the sign of the input gradient
FGSM
Many small steps, each projected back into the budget
PGD
Examples crafted on a substitute model fool the target
Transfer attack
Only the predicted label is returned, yet the attack works
Decision-based attack
A record’s loss is compared under models trained with and without it

blocks.title: Robustness evaluation terms
cards: Perturbation budget (ε)
The largest change an attacker is allowed, measured with a norm such as L∞ or L2.
Obfuscated gradients
A defence that breaks gradient-based attacks without making the model robust; adaptive attacks get around it.
Adaptive attack
An attack designed with full knowledge of the specific defence, the standard for credible robustness claims.
AutoAttack
An ensemble of parameter-free attacks used as a reliable benchmark for adversarial robustness.
Shadow model
A model the attacker trains on similar data, with known members, to learn what membership looks like.
TPR at low FPR
The share of true members found while false positives stay very rare, the preferred measure for membership inference.

q.q: A vendor reports that its image classifier keeps 85% accuracy under attack. The evaluation used FGSM only, and accuracy barely changed as the budget grew. What is the BEST response?
o: Accept the result, as FGSM is a recognised and widely published attack
Ask for adaptive, iterative attacks, as the results suggest gradient masking
Ask for the test to be repeated with a smaller perturbation budget
Reject the model, as robust accuracy must always exceed 90% under attack
q.why: A single weak attack, and accuracy that doesn’t fall as the budget grows, are classic signs of obfuscated gradients. Credible claims need strong iterative and adaptive attacks across a range of budgets. A smaller budget would make the test weaker, and there is no universal 90% rule.

quiz.q: What is PASTA’s main distinguishing feature as a threat modelling method?
o: It focuses only on privacy threats to personal data held in systems
A risk-centric, seven-stage process tied to business objectives
It can only be used for agentic AI systems with multiple agents
It replaces data flow diagrams with fully automated code scanning
quiz.why: PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) links threats and attack simulations to business impact through seven stages.

quiz.q: What does MAESTRO add for agentic systems?
o: A scoring system for the severity of software vulnerabilities
Seven layers to analyse, including threats that cross between layers
A certification scheme for agent developers and their organisations
A list of approved foundation models for use in agent frameworks
quiz.why: MAESTRO decomposes agentic systems into seven layers and highlights cross-layer threats, such as poisoned memory hijacking tools.

quiz.q: Why should AI threat models cover the whole pipeline, not just the deployed application?
o: Regulators only accept threat models that are longer than fifty pages
Data sourcing, training, registries and deployment have their own threats
Applications built on AI never contain any security weaknesses
Pipeline threats are always more serious than application threats
quiz.why: Poisoning, backdoors, model swaps and pipeline compromise happen before the application ever runs.

quiz.q: Which four attacker goals does NIST AI 100-2 use?
o: Speed, scale, stealth and simplicity
Availability, integrity, privacy and misuse enablement
Reconnaissance, access, execution and exfiltration
Confidentiality, authentication, authorisation and audit
quiz.why: NIST’s adversarial ML taxonomy classifies attacks by these goals, with misuse enablement specific to generative AI.

quiz.q: Which actor combines the most dangerous access and capability for AI systems?
o: An opportunistic user trying jailbreaks found online
A malicious insider with machine learning skills
A careless employee using a public chatbot
A competitor reading the company’s published model card
quiz.why: Legitimate access plus the skill to poison data, plant backdoors or copy weights makes skilled malicious insiders especially dangerous.

quiz.q: Why should agents and tools be considered potential threat actors in threat models?
o: Agents are always deliberately malicious, because of how they are designed
If compromised, they act with legitimate permissions at machine speed
Tools can’t be secured, so they must be removed from all systems
Threat models are required to include at least one non-human actor
quiz.why: A hijacked agent or malicious tool can do anything its permissions allow, very quickly, which drives least agency and monitoring.

quiz.q: At which stage does an evasion attack take place?
o: During data collection, before any training has begun
At inference, using crafted inputs to a deployed model
During training, through corrupted or flipped labels
In the model registry, by swapping the model files
quiz.why: Evasion manipulates inputs to a deployed model; poisoning and backdoors happen at training time.

quiz.q: Why do backdoors often survive normal model evaluation?
o: Evaluation suites never test language models
The trigger is rare, so clean accuracy looks normal
Backdoors only activate during the evaluation itself
Evaluation is always skipped for fine-tuned models
quiz.why: Without the trigger, a backdoored model behaves normally, so standard test sets don’t reveal it.

quiz.q: Which control MOST directly reduces the risk of model extraction?
o: Encrypting the training data at rest in the data lake
Rate limiting and returning only the minimum output detail
Adding more layers to the neural network architecture
Publishing the model card, including full architecture details
quiz.why: Extraction depends on many queries and detailed outputs, so limiting both slows or prevents it.

quiz.q: What did the PoisonedRAG research show?
o: RAG systems can’t be poisoned if the model is large enough
A handful of crafted documents can steer answers in a huge knowledge base
Poisoning only works when attackers control the embedding model
Knowledge bases holding millions of documents are effectively immune to poisoning
quiz.why: Five crafted texts per target question, among millions, achieved around 90% attack success, and tested defences were insufficient.

o: A package manager installing the wrong version of a library
A model inventing a package name that attackers can then register
A library that produces random outputs during automated testing
Duplicate packages appearing in a software bill of materials
quiz.why: Hallucinated package names recur, so attackers can register them with malicious code ("slopsquatting").

quiz.q: Which OWASP agentic risk describes planted instructions in an agent’s persistent memory?
o: Agent goal hijack (ASI01)
Memory and context poisoning (ASI06)
Insecure inter-agent communication (ASI07)
Cascading failures (ASI08)
quiz.why: ASI06, memory and context poisoning, covers corrupted memory or shared context that affects later work.

quiz.q: What is the BEST defence against deepfake requests for urgent payments?
o: Training staff to spot the visual glitches that reveal fakes in calls
Verifying through a separate known channel, with dual approval
Requiring executives to keep their cameras on during calls
Using the newest video conferencing software available
quiz.why: Process controls work however convincing the fake; spotting glitches becomes harder as deepfakes improve.

quiz.q: Why can AI availability attacks succeed without large traffic floods?
o: AI systems have no rate limits of any kind, by design
Single requests can be very costly in tokens and compute
Floods are blocked automatically by every model provider
AI systems always run on a single server with no redundancy
quiz.why: Context stuffing, output amplification and agent loops make individual requests expensive.

o: A training example designed to absorb labelling errors from others
An input crafted to maximise a model’s computation and latency
A small, clean dataset used to dilute poisoned records
A prompt that makes a model forget its earlier instructions
quiz.why: Sponge examples, described in 2021 research, target energy use and latency, an availability attack.

quiz.q: What distinguishes PGD from FGSM when crafting adversarial examples?
o: PGD needs only the model’s labels, while FGSM needs its gradients
PGD takes many small steps, projecting back into the budget each time
PGD changes a few pixels a lot, while FGSM changes all pixels a little
PGD works only on text models, while FGSM works only on image models
quiz.why: FGSM takes a single step along the sign of the input gradient. PGD iterates many smaller steps from a random start, projecting back inside the budget after each, which makes it a much stronger attack.

quiz.q: An attacker can’t query a target model before an attack, but has an openly available model trained on similar data. Which approach is MOST practical?
o: A decision-based attack, walking along the target’s boundary
A transfer attack, using examples crafted on the open model
A score-based attack, estimating gradients from confidence
A membership inference attack, using shadow models of it
quiz.why: Adversarial examples often transfer between models trained for similar tasks, so the attacker can craft them on the open model without querying the target. Score-based and decision-based attacks need queries.

quiz.q: Why do researchers report membership inference results as the true-positive rate at a low false-positive rate?
o: Average accuracy is always 50%, so it can’t distinguish between attacks
Confidently identifying even a few individuals is the real privacy harm
Low false-positive rates make attacks run faster on large datasets
Regulators require that exact metric in every privacy impact assessment
quiz.why: An attack can look weak on average yet identify some people with high confidence, which is what matters for privacy. Carlini and colleagues argued for this measure when introducing LiRA.

quiz.q: Which sign MOST suggests that a defence relies on obfuscated gradients?
o: Accuracy under attack falls steadily to zero as the budget grows
Single-step attacks succeed more often than iterative attacks do
Clean accuracy is a few points lower than the undefended model’s
The defence was evaluated with AutoAttack and adaptive attacks
quiz.why: Iterative attacks should be at least as strong as single-step ones. When they do worse, the defence is probably breaking gradient-based attacks rather than resisting them, and adaptive attacks are likely to succeed.

exam.q: A bank is building a customer-facing agent that can move money. The security architect needs a threat modelling approach that links threats to business impact and supports detailed attack simulation. Which is MOST appropriate?
o: LINDDUN, because customer data is involved
PASTA, supplemented with MAESTRO for the agent’s layers
A STRIDE review of the login page only
No threat model, since the vendor has certified the agent platform
exam.why: PASTA ties threats to business impact through attack simulation, and MAESTRO covers agent-specific layers. LINDDUN is privacy-focused, a login-only review is too narrow, and vendor certification doesn’t replace a threat model.

exam.q: A threat model for an AI system was completed at design time two years ago. Since then, the system has gained web browsing, a new vector database and three new tools. What should happen?
o: Nothing, because the original threat model was approved by the architecture board
Update the threat model for the new components, data flows and trust boundaries
Remove the new capabilities, so that the original threat model remains valid
Commission a penetration test instead, as threat models become outdated
exam.why: Threat models must evolve with the system; new tools and data sources add trust boundaries and threats. Testing complements threat modelling rather than replacing it.

exam.q: Which scenario BEST describes a non-human threat actor?
o: An employee who forgets to lock their laptop in a café
An agent hijacked by injected content, acting with its own permissions
A competitor who carefully reads all of the company’s published research papers
A contractor who works remotely from another country
exam.why: A hijacked agent acts against the organisation using its own legitimate access, which is why agents belong in threat models as potential adversaries.

exam.q: An ML engineer downloads full model weights to a personal cloud storage account two days before resigning. Which control set would MOST likely have prevented or detected this?
o: Annual security awareness training for all engineering staff
Least privilege on weights, with DLP and monitoring of downloads
A non-disclosure agreement signed on the engineer’s first day
Encrypting weights at rest with a key the engineer could access
exam.why: Restricting access, blocking or flagging transfers to personal storage, and monitoring downloads address the insider path. Training and NDAs deter but don’t stop it, and accessible keys don’t help.

exam.q: Attackers have discovered they can slightly modify malware so that a security vendor’s ML classifier labels it benign. What type of attack is this, and which defence is MOST relevant?
o: Poisoning; retrain the classifier on its original, unmodified training data
Evasion; adversarial training and robustness testing of the classifier
Model extraction; remove the classifier from all public download sites
Membership inference; apply differential privacy during training
exam.why: Crafted inputs that fool a deployed model are evasion; adversarial training and robustness testing improve resistance. The other attack types don’t match the scenario.

exam.q: A healthcare model’s API returns detailed confidence scores, and researchers show they can infer whether specific patients were in its training data. Which mitigation BEST addresses this?
o: Increase the model’s accuracy so that its predictions are more reliable
Reduce output detail, and retrain the model with differential privacy
Move the model to a faster GPU cluster to reduce response times
Add a disclaimer to every response about the use of patient data
exam.why: Membership inference exploits detailed outputs and overfitting; reducing output detail and differential privacy directly limit it.

exam.q: A legal research assistant retrieves from a large public case-law corpus that anyone can contribute to. Which threat should be prioritised in its threat model?
o: Model extraction through very high volumes of API queries from partners
Knowledge poisoning through crafted documents added to the corpus
Physical theft of the servers that host the vector database
Typographic attacks using text embedded in images
exam.why: Open contribution makes knowledge poisoning and injection carriers the primary risk, and research shows a few crafted documents can steer answers.

exam.q: A procurement agent accepted fabricated supplier "facts" from a research agent and initiated payments, which a human approved because both agents agreed. Which OWASP agentic risks are MOST evident?
o: Unexpected code execution, and rogue agents acting alone
Cascading failures and human-agent trust exploitation
Agentic supply chain flaws and insecure inter-agent messages
Identity abuse and unexpected code execution
exam.why: An error spreading from one agent to another is a cascading failure, and approval based on the agents’ agreement is human-agent trust exploitation.

exam.q: An insurer’s claims assistant accepts photos of damage. Testers find that text written on a photographed object can change the assistant’s assessment. What is the BEST response?
o: Stop accepting photos, and require customers to describe damage in text
Treat text found in images as untrusted input, and validate assessments
Increase the image resolution, so the model reads the text more accurately
Train customers not to include any text in the photos they submit
exam.why: This is a typographic injection; all modalities are untrusted input, and assessments need validation. Banning photos loses value, and higher resolution or customer training doesn’t stop attackers.

exam.q: A startup’s public chatbot is hit by a few accounts sending maximum-length prompts that trigger long agent workflows. Monthly costs triple. Which control would have limited the damage MOST?
o: A web application firewall with signatures for known attack strings
Per-account quotas, input and output caps, and per-task agent budgets
A larger committed-use discount negotiated with the model provider
Moving the chatbot to a different cloud region with more capacity
exam.why: Quotas, token caps and agent budgets directly bound the cost each account and task can incur. Signatures, discounts and more capacity don’t limit abuse.

exam.q: Why is cost per hour often the earliest signal of an AI availability attack?
o: Providers send cost alerts before any other monitoring signal exists
Attacks can use few, expensive requests that barely change traffic volume
Cost data is the only telemetry most AI platforms bother to collect
Network monitoring tools can’t see any of the traffic sent to AI services
exam.why: Resource exhaustion often comes from a small number of costly requests, so token and cost metrics move before traffic volume does.

exam.q: A fraud detection API returns a score from 0 to 100 for each transaction. Attackers are probing it to find the smallest changes that avoid detection. Which change would MOST raise the cost of this attack?
o: Publishing the model card, so partners understand its limitations
Returning only an approve or review decision, with query limits
Increasing the score’s precision from whole numbers to decimals
Retraining the model monthly on the latest legitimate transactions
exam.why: Detailed scores let attackers estimate gradients; returning only a decision forces slower decision-based attacks, and query limits and monitoring cap the probing. More precision would help the attacker.

exam.q: A hospital wants to know whether its published diagnostic model reveals which patients were in its training data. Which test BEST answers this?
o: An evasion test, using PGD attacks at several perturbation budgets
A membership inference test, measured at a low false-positive rate
A reproducibility test, checking that answers repeat across runs
A fairness test, comparing accuracy across different patient groups
exam.why: Membership inference directly tests whether someone can tell that a record was used in training, and measuring at a low false-positive rate shows whether individuals can be identified confidently.

exam.q: During threat modelling, an architect notes that anyone can download the open-source base model the company fine-tuned for its content filter. Which risk does this MOST increase?
o: Model inversion, since the base model contains the company’s fine-tuning data
Transfer attacks, since examples crafted on the base model may also work
Denial of service, since attackers can run the same model at a large scale
Licence breach, since fine-tuned models can’t be used commercially
exam.why: A fine-tuned model stays close to its base, so adversarial inputs crafted on the public base model are likely to transfer. The base model doesn’t contain the company’s fine-tuning data.
